narrative: The model estimated a 52.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means it judged failure slightly more likely than passing—not certain—and that estimate placed you on the failure side of the admission decision, so your law school application was denied. The strongest factor was your third-year class-standing decile: at 2, well below the accepted-student average of about 5.8, it pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other item. Your first-year decile, at 1 versus an accepted average near 6, was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor; although it was below the accepted average of about 37.2 at 35.5, its influence leaned toward passing rather than failing. The two decile signals outweighed that positive signal, leaving the model just above the failure line. To strengthen a future application, focus on demonstrating sustained academic improvement, meet with admissions advising about how to contextualize your early grades, and consider whether retaking the LSAT could add margin. You should also discuss alternative programs or pathways with a counselor and request feedback from the program.
